rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an and Torah do not specify whether Moses completed eight or ten years of service.
rows.anchor: It is not specified either by the Qur’ ān or the Torah whether the term completed was eight years or ten.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah indicates Moses traveled with his wife and two children to the mount of Ṭūr on a dark, cold night.
rows.anchor: with his two children besides his wife, when they reached the mount of Ṭūr, the night was dark and it was cold too.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In darkness, Moses saw a light on the mountain and asked his family to wait while he sought people for directions or an ember for warmth.
rows.anchor: he saw something shining from the side of the mount of Ṭūr. He told his wife and children to stay there

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessed valley, blessed area, and tree specify a clear, known source for the voice Moses heard.
rows.anchor: the purpose of all these determinants is that Moses (sws) did not hear this voice from some vague or ambiguous origin.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sacred tree in a blessed place and holy valley signals God’s chosen manifestation; such a place is pure, secure, and frequented by angels.
rows.anchor: such an area be the place where His angels frequent and which is totally pure and secure.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The voice first identifies God as Lord of the worlds, an expansive expression explained elsewhere as God the Powerful and Wise.
rows.anchor: It is Me, God, the Powerful, the Wise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets encounter the beginning of prophethood suddenly and without seeking it, so they initially feel worry before God gradually accustoms them to it.
rows.anchor: Neither do they have any concept about it nor do they have any desire for it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Soothsayers and magicians plan routines to mislead people and treat a successful deception as a great achievement, unlike God’s prophets.
rows.anchor: they already have a scheme in their minds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Egyptians’ celebrated magic made staffs and ropes look like serpents through arduous routines; Moses’ fear at God’s real miracle exposes the difference.
rows.anchor: staffs and ropes into serpents.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God tenderly reassures Moses to approach and take up the staff; the danger is for his enemy, while God’s messengers are secure in His presence.
rows.anchor: He was secure from every form of peril.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ second sign is a hand placed in his armpit that emerges pure white, with no illness causing the whiteness.
rows.anchor: press your hand towards your armpit; it will emerge white from there without any illness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The instruction to draw the arm back as from fear describes pressing the hand into the armpit, as stated in 20:22.
rows.anchor: And press your hand towards your armpit; it will emerge white from there without any illness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase مِنَ الرَّهْب is an idiomatic construction also found with مِنَ الذُّل and مِنَ الرَّحْمَة.
rows.anchor: at other instances in the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A verb is omitted before ذَانِكَ; the implied command is to go warn Pharaoh and his people with the two clear signs.
rows.anchor: A verb is suppressed before

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses asks God to send his more eloquent brother Aaron as a helper because he fears rejection and wants both of them to convey the truth forcefully.
rows.anchor: both of them could convey the truth conclusively with full force.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses fears that Pharaoh’s people will reject his message; Aaron’s eloquence would help the brothers communicate the truth forcefully.
rows.anchor: both of them could convey the truth conclusively with full force.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here sulṭān means dominance, majesty, and awe; the signs may either create awe through miracles or follow a suppressed verb.
rows.anchor: here means “dominance, majesty and awe.” There are two possibilities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God accepts Aaron’s help and assures both brothers that Pharaoh’s people will not harm them; they feared Moses as truthful despite rejecting his message for self-interest.
rows.anchor: the Pharaoh and his people were so over-awed by Moses (sws) that, in spite of their desire to get rid of him, they could not dare do so.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s people called Moses’ clear signs magic and campaigned against his monotheistic message as contrary to their ancestors’ traditions.
rows.anchor: they regarded these to be a product of magic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their claim that they had never heard of such a thing refers to Moses’ claim to be God’s messenger and his call to monotheism, as echoed in 38:7.
rows.anchor: we have not heard of this in this later period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses says God knows who succeeds in the Hereafter; those who deny guidance wrong themselves and cannot succeed.
rows.anchor: It is certain that those who deny the guidance sent by God will be unjust to themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hāmān held the rank of prime minister or at least a minister responsible for construction and development at Pharaoh’s court.
rows.anchor: he had the same status in the court of the Pharaoh as that of a prime minister or at least a minister of construction and development.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction phrase can mean making a brick kiln or building a clay structure and firing it; heated mud construction was common in Egypt and Nineveh.
rows.anchor: a common way of construction in Nineveh and Egypt was to build a house with mud and then have it heated strongly with flames.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction wording contains taḍmīn, implying Pharaoh would climb the building and peer at Moses’ God as a mocking gesture.
rows.anchor: Obviously, these words were meant to make fun of Moses (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh claims there is no god for his people but himself and ridicules Moses’ God; autocrats’ mockery can be mistaken by followers for proof.
rows.anchor: at times, autocrats and tyrants make fun of absolutely evident facts in this way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s followers may have taken his mockery literally because they regarded him as an avatar of the Sun God; his tower scheme may have deceived the masses.
rows.anchor: they regarded the Pharaoh to be an avatar of their Sun God. How could it be difficult for an avatar to take a peep

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only the Creator and governor of heaven and earth has a right to arrogance; human arrogance is baseless, and disobeying the true King’s law follows Pharaoh’s example.
rows.anchor: Only the One Who has created the heavens and the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh and his army’s belief that they would never return to God explains their arrogance: they expected no accountability.
rows.anchor: they thought that God would let them go without questioning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A curse followed the arrogant wrongdoers in this world as they led people astray.
rows.anchor: The verse states the Almighty made curse follow them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to consider the unjust people’s fate directs attention to the lesson of the account and reassures the Prophet against arrogant opponents of his message.
rows.anchor: They sound an assurance to the Prophet (sws) and remind and warn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb “made” includes the sense of granting respite, and an incomplete verb is suppressed before “they call.”
rows.anchor: here encompasses the meaning of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gave them worldly respite as leaders calling people to Hell; on Judgment Day neither leaders nor followers will help one another.
rows.anchor: God gave them respite in this world and they

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A curse followed them in this world and they will be humiliated in the Hereafter, as explained in 11:97–98.
rows.anchor: On the Day of Judgement, he will be in front of his nation and will land them into the Fire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the cited account, the Pharaoh led his people toward the Fire and was an evil leader.
rows.anchor: So, they followed the opinion of the Pharaoh and the opinion of the Pharaoh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book is insight because it develops reflection and understanding; when guidance and mercy occur together, they refer respectively to this life and the next.
rows.anchor: the capability to reflect and deliberate.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Receiving God’s Book and law confers religious and political leadership conditionally on valuing the gift; Israel received it first but treated it contemptuously.
rows.anchor: this is conditional to giving due value to this gift of God’s book.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing verses address Muhammad and implicitly Jews and Quraysh, validating his prophethood because he was absent when Moses received the Torah.
rows.anchor: actually directed to the Jews and to the Quraysh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “western side” means the western side of Mount Ṭūr; qadaynā carries the sense of making a covenant, as at 2:125.
rows.anchor: A similar usage is found in

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “witnesses” are Moses’ people waiting at the mountain while he went alone for the Torah; the Samiri incident occurred then, and these details evidence revelation to Muhammad.
rows.anchor: This is a reference to the time when Moses (sws) had left his people at the base of the mountain and in accordance with the divine directive had gone alone to receive the Torah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s detailed account of Moses is coherent and preserves essential elements, whereas the Torah’s account is incoherent, interpolated, and missing or distorting them.
rows.anchor: of the Torah is totally incoherent and interpolated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account could not have come from contemporaneous People of the Book: hearsay should follow their general telling, while the Qur’an’s version exposes itself as true to fair-minded readers.
rows.anchor: every fair minded person cries out that the true version of the incident is the one which the Qur’ ān has described

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After generations passed and people forgot God’s guidance, God informed Muhammad of these events to revive that guidance through him.
rows.anchor: a great time lapsed and people forgot this book of Ours which was sent as guidance and mercy; hence, it was essential that We revive this guidance through you.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet was absent from Madyan and did not know Moses’ experiences there or Shu‘ayb’s mission and people’s fate; God made him aware as a messenger.
rows.anchor: he was not present in Madyan

none: Work title and sūra heading only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah al-Rūm is the counterpart of al-‘Ankabūt; their shared Alif Lām Mīm name reflects similar central themes.
rows.anchor: This sūrah is the counterpart of the previous sūrah: al-‘Ankabūt. Both have the same Qur’ānic name: Alif Lām Mīm.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding sūra promises believers divine help and supremacy, grounded in purposeful creation, God’s control, the Hereafter, perfect justice, and the truth’s lasting victory.
rows.anchor: In the previous sūrah, in spite of the apparent trying circumstances, Muslims are given glad tidings of divine help and supremacy.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The 614 defeat of Roman Christians by Magians in Syria and Palestine polarized Muslims and Arabian idolaters; the latter took it as proof against Qur’anic claims and mocked them.
rows.anchor: in their neighbourhood in 614 AD the Magians attacked the Roman occupied lands of Syria and Palestine and expelled them from there.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an uses this event to restate the truths the idolaters had challenged.
rows.anchor: Through this event, the Qur’ān has once again delineated the facts which the Idolaters had cast doubt upon.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–7 frame Roman defeat and promised victory as part of God’s just, established pattern for nations, which superficial observers fail to grasp.
rows.anchor: the rise and fall of nations in this world are not incidental happenings. They occur on the basis of an established practice of the Almighty which is based on justice.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 8–18 argue that purposeful creation and historical judgment make the Hereafter inevitable; believers will win, false intercessors will fail, and all creation glorifies God.
rows.anchor: its creator has not created it as a place of amusement and entertainment. Hence, it will necessarily culminate on a day of reward and punishment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 19–29 draw arguments from human beings and the outer world to establish monotheism and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Arguments drawn from the world inside man and the one external to him are proffered to substantiate the beliefs of monotheism and the hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 30–45 call the Prophet to the religion of human nature, prayer, and zakāh, admonish those who distort it, and urge perseverance while awaiting God’s judgment.
rows.anchor: This religion is based on the institutions of the prayer and the zakāh. Those who have perverted this religion are admonished

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 46–60 cite historical proof of divine help; only people of intellect receive the message, so the Prophet must persevere and await God’s promise despite stubborn rejection.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is assured that his message can touch the hearts of those people only who have intellect.

none: Qur’anic translation text only; no authorial commentary.
